isolation.scenario: Build the kernel module and load it: this is an ordinary virtual machine with its own kernel, root, Docker and a real SSH port, not a shared user-space sandbox.
isolation.note: A full KVM virtual machine per Instance with its own kernel, disk and public IP. Docker is a one-click InstantApp and any container runtime can be installed. Nested virtualisation is not documented either way, the hypervisor is never named, and GPU Instances are a separate, much more expensive range.

source.quote: An Instance is a virtual machine in the cloud. Like a physical machine, it provides resources such as virtualized CPU, RAM, and storage.

sizes-regions.scenario: The 4 vCPU / 8 GiB ask fits DEV1-L, PLAY2-MICRO or BASIC3-X4C-8G exactly, in Paris, Amsterdam, Warsaw or Milan, and the machine can be moved to another offer later with a reboot.
sizes-regions.note: Fixed offers only: shared and development ranges run from 1 vCPU / 1 GiB to 48 vCPU / 256 GiB, with dedicated STANDARD3 and POP2 up to 64 vCPU outside this card. Disk is separate, up to 15 TB per block volume and 600 GB of local SSD. No custom CPU/RAM split, no live resize, and not every offer exists in every zone.

source.quote: vCPUs 48 vCPU type Shared RAM size 256 GiB

lifecycle.figure: Off stops compute; disk and IP stay
lifecycle.scenario: At 18:00 the Instance is powered off: the REPL, the dev server and the cron job are gone, but the disk and the IP address are still there at 09:00, and only the 90 running hours are billed for compute.
lifecycle.note: Powering off releases the hypervisor and stops compute billing; attached storage and any reserved flexible IPv4 keep billing. Local storage can be kept or archived on stop. There is no memory-preserving pause, and standby mode keeps the machine allocated but is billed in full, so it saves nothing.

source.quote: Compute billing stops, but you continue to pay for any attached storage (local volumes that you chose to keep or Block Storage volumes) and for any Flexible IPs.

snapshots-forks.figure: Disk snapshots; no memory, no fork
snapshots-forks.scenario: Snapshot the volume before the risky refactor and boot a new Instance from it if the change goes wrong; the half-written files are there, the queued test run in memory is not.
snapshots-forks.note: Volume snapshots and whole-Instance images are manual, kept until deleted, and can be exported or imported as QCOW2. They never include RAM, there is no copy-on-write fork of a running machine, and there is no automatic backup schedule: Scaleway documents a do-it-yourself one built on Serverless Jobs. Snapshots bill at €0.000049/GB/hour.

source.quote: Creating an image makes a complete backup of your Instance, including all of its volumes.

storage.scenario: Postgres writes to /var/lib and is still there at 08:00, because the whole volume is persistent and billed by its provisioned size whether the machine runs or not.
storage.note: Two storage designs: block volumes (network-attached, 5 GB to 15 TB, up to 16 per Instance, persistent without the machine) and local SSD on DEV1, GP1 and STARDUST1 (up to 600 GB, tied to the host, kept or archived on stop). The boot volume must be at least 10 GB. Object Storage is S3-compatible but has no native mount.

source.quote: Block volumes provide network-attached storage you can plug in/out of Instances like a virtual hard drive.

idle-timers.figure: No idle timer or session limit
idle-timers.scenario: At 00:20 the machine is still running and still billing, with the queued test run intact; nothing in the product will stop it for being quiet.
idle-timers.note: There is no idle timeout, auto-stop or maximum session length, so an always-on agent is safe from the provider but pays for every idle hour. The same absence means there is no wake path: a stopped Instance stays stopped until something calls the API, and standby mode bills in full.

source.quote: The Instance is fully active and consumes compute resources.

reaching-it.scenario: The demo on port 3000 is reachable at a static public address with no token in front of it, so anyone with the link gets through and the security group is the only filter.
reaching-it.note: A flexible IPv4 routed to the Instance, a free flexible IPv6, any port opened through a stateful or stateless security group, and a real SSH daemon. There is no provider-issued preview or private token URL, and the browser console is a serial TTY for troubleshooting rather than a day-to-day shell.

source.quote: Flexible routed IPv4 addresses: public IPv4 addresses routed directly to your Instance.

custom-domains.figure: Your DNS; TLS via LB or Caddy
custom-domains.scenario: Point an A record at the static IP and run Caddy on the machine for a certificate; there is no per-Instance domain mapping or managed certificate.
custom-domains.note: A fixed public IP makes a custom domain a DNS record, and Scaleway sells Domains and DNS. Managed Let's Encrypt certificates belong to the Load Balancer and Edge Services, which front a Load Balancer, Object Storage or a Serverless Container, not an Instance directly. On a plain Instance you install and renew the certificate yourself.

source.quote: You can choose between uploading your own certificate held in Scaleway Secret Manager, or letting Edge Services generate a fully-managed Let's Encrypt certificate.

outbound-network.scenario: The agent browses freely with no per-GB bill, inside the shape's bandwidth, and outbound security-group rules can restrict where it goes.
outbound-network.note: Instance list prices include egress and Scaleway states there are no egress fees; the meter is the shape's public bandwidth, 100 Mbps to 16 Gbps. Security groups filter outbound traffic as well as inbound, an Instance can be created without a public IPv4, and a private network gives it no internet path.

source.quote: List prices include egress and IPv6 addresses.

keys-secrets.scenario: The model key sits in Secret Manager or in a file on the machine, and anything running on the machine can read it; there is no write-only store.
keys-secrets.note: Secret Manager is a separate product with versioned, path-scoped secrets, ephemeral policies, single-access secrets and a TTL of up to a year. It is not injected into an Instance at boot, and there is no proxy that lets the agent use a key it cannot read. API keys are properly scoped through IAM policies and permission sets.

source.quote: An ephemeral secret is a secret that has a limited lifetime, enforced by an ephemeral policy.

ways-to-drive.scenario: The first machine is clickable in the console; everything after that is scriptable through the API, the scw CLI or the Python, Go and TypeScript SDKs.
ways-to-drive.note: Console wizard, documented REST API with OpenAPI specs, official CLI and SDKs for Python, Go and JavaScript/TypeScript, plus a Terraform provider. No official MCP server, no PTY endpoint and no file API, so an agent driving the platform uses HTTP or SSH.

source.quote: Manage your resources with the Scaleway API using simple HTTP requests.

built-in-agents.figure: None; Docker and web apps only
built-in-agents.scenario: Nothing is preinstalled: the agent is your install, your systemd unit and your updates.
built-in-agents.note: InstantApps are Docker, GitLab, Nextcloud, WordPress and OpenVPN, and the Marketplace adds more infrastructure images. No coding agent, no Hermes, no OpenClaw, no prompt API and no browser image. Scaleway's OpenClaw content is about pointing OpenClaw at its Generative APIs from a local machine or Mac mini, not hosting the Gateway on an Instance.

source.quote: An InstantApp allows you to deploy pre-configured applications quickly on CPU Instances.

teams-accounts.figure: IAM, SAML SSO, audit; alerts not caps
teams-accounts.scenario: Five developers share an Organization with projects, permission sets, SAML SSO and an audit trail, but nothing stops a runaway machine when the budget is reached.
teams-accounts.note: Organizations, Projects, Members, groups, applications, fine-grained permission sets with CEL conditions, SAML SSO with SCIM, and Audit Trail with a 90-day export. Billing alerts only notify: there is no hard spending cap, and default per-type Instance quotas are small rather than spend-based.

source.quote: Permissions sets and their scope make up IAM rules, which define the access rights that a principal (user, group or application) should have.

billing-models.scenario: A machine that mostly waits still pays for every hour it is powered on, but a machine that is switched off between sessions pays only storage and its IPv4, not the reserved shape.
billing-models.note: The meter is the allocated shape by the hour of uptime, with a 60-minute minimum per resource per start and stop, and no monthly cap. Powering off stops compute billing while storage and a reserved flexible IPv4 continue. That makes idle time cheap compared with a VPS that bills while off, but short tasks expensive compared with per-second sandboxes.

source.quote: Each of these resources is billed separately for a minimum of 60 minutes.

trials-free-tiers.scenario: A new Business account with a card can start with €100 of credit, but there is no free Instance size and the card stays on the account afterwards.
trials-free-tiers.note: New Business customers with a valid payment method and no prior Scaleway invoice receive a €100 voucher by email within 24 hours, which must be redeemed. No ongoing free tier covers Instances, prepaid cards are refused, and a card is required even when SEPA is used.

source.quote: Create a Business account and get started with €100 free credit.

company.scenario: The buyer can check a French company with a published legal notice, ISO 27001 and HDS certifications, an online DPA and a 99% SLO on BASIC3, but gets no SLA at all on the cheap ranges.
company.note: Scaleway SAS of Paris, a subsidiary of the iliad Group, operating four EU regions. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and HDS certified, SecNumCloud under assessment, DPA published with the contracts, public status page. The Instance SLA gives 99% to BASIC3-X and BASIC2-A, 99.5% to dedicated ranges, and no SLO to DEV1, GP1, PLAY2 or PRO2. No SOC 2 is listed.

source.quote: Scaleway is committed to obtaining the most stringent certifications (ISO 27001, HDS, SecNumCloud – currently undergoing assessment)
